   CITY OF BEVERLY HILLS

  FIRE DEPARTMENT

  MEMORANDUM

TO:  Social Services Council Liaisons

FROM:  Christopher Paulson, Deputy Director of Community Services

  Stephanie Harris, Director of Community Services

  Gregory Barton, Fire Chief

DATE:  October 30, 2024

SUBJECT:  COMMUNITY ASSISTANCE GRANT FUNDING:  CURRENT  AND
  FUTURE NEEDS AND RECOMMENDED CHANGES

ATTACHMENTS: A – Current CAGF Funding Amounts
  B – Proposed Funding Amounts

INTRODUCTION

 Maintaining a social service safety net is a public service priority stated in the City’s General Plan. The
City’s Community Assistance Grant Funding (CAGF) enables the City to secure partnerships with local
social service agencies to support the quality of life of Beverly Hills’ residents. The City’s Safety
Network creates a continuum of care for the most vulnerable members of the community including
active and frail elderly residents, disabled individuals, residents of little to low means, and unhoused
individuals. The Fire Department’s Human Services Division administers the CAGF program.
The City’s CAGF program was created several decades ago and was intended to be a way in which the
City can provide funding to organizations to provide a particular social service needed by some
members of the community, that could be delivered more effectively through a non-profit organization,
rather than using City staff.
Many conditions in Beverly Hills and society in general has changed since the CAGF program was first
created, which may render some legacy grants less impactful today than they were 20 years ago.
Additionally, many of the non-profit service providers are able to offer their services to Beverly Hills
residents, and regional residents, in need without receiving the corresponding funding from the City of
Beverly Hills.
Additionally, the CAGF budget has continued to increase, while at the same time the City Council is
seeking to reduce costs throughout the organization where appropriate without reducing the service
delivery. The total cost in general fund monies for Fiscal Year 2022-23 was $2,020,000, that rose to
$2,077,500 in 2023-24, and again to $2,406,143 in the current year 2024-25.
This report seeks to discuss possible changes to the CAGF process as implemented in the current
2024-25 agreement year, and further changes to the program structure going forward, to ensure that
costs are controlled, services continue to be delivered to the community, and that services are provided

10/30/2024 Social Services Liaisons
 specifically to Beverly Hills residents and not simply the greater region. As the Human Services division
was transferred to the Fire Department from the Community Services Department earlier this year, staff
is looking at community health as a whole and the role the CAGF program plays in delivering social
services through a community health model.

DISCUSSION

The Human Relations Commission has historically reviewed CAGF proposals and provided grant
funding recommendations to the City Council, with the assistance of the Charitable Solicitations
Commission. The Commissions agreed that the safety network that the current CAGF funding provides
to the community is extremely vital at this time, and that it was important, at a minimum, to try to keep
all funding at least at the same level as the current fiscal year where appropriate. In some cases, it was
warranted to decrease the funding level in accordance with the new fiscal year budget.

There was also a substantial update to the CAGF process this year, five critical service providers were
moved to direct contractual relationships with the city, based on services rendered, for the current fiscal
year. These organizations include Jewish Family Services Los Angeles, Beverly Hills CPR, People
Assisting the Homeless (P.A.T.H.), Step Up on Second, and Bet Tzedek Legal Services. The not-to-
exceed amount to contract with these five organizations for Fiscal Year 2024-25 is $1,292,643.
The City prioritizes funding for services to benefit the most vulnerable members of the community.
Active and frail elderly, disabled individuals, residents of little to low means, and unhoused individuals
continue to be the primary populations in need of assistance. The City targets services through CAGF
that address these populations’ special needs.

2024-25 Updated CAGF Process
Critical Service Providers
This year, staff recommended a slightly different process, by sorting the organizations into two groups
and removing one of those groups from the CAGF process. The first group of organizations are those
that provide crucial services to the community and cannot be replicated by City-staff. Serious
unintended consequences may be experienced by residents should services not be made available.
The City has entered into contractual agreements for services rendered, based on billable hours for
Beverly Hills residents, separately and outside of the CAGF process.

There are five critical service providers that moved towards direct contracts with the city, based on
services rendered, for the fiscal year. These organizations include Jewish Family Services Los Angeles
($505,000), Beverly Hills CPR ($75,000), People Assisting the Homeless (P.A.T.H.) ($100,000), Step
Up on Second ($392,643), and Bet Tzedek Legal Services ($220,000). The total amount to contract
with these five organizations for Fiscal Year 24/25 is $1,292,643.

CAGF Partners
The next group of organizations, which are the bulk of grantees, are those that provide a General
Social Service Program that provides quality of life services to the community that are otherwise not
being provided; services are not urgent in nature and no serious consequences are present should
services be delayed. This group also contains a few organizations that provide Cultural Arts Programs.
This is the group that will participate in the CAGF process.

  2
10/30/2024 Social Services Liaisons
 Some additional criteria and metrics that were requested through the application process and in the
quarterly reporting is a focus on direct referrals for services from Beverly Hills residents, or Beverly Hills
staff, to ensure these grants benefit the Beverly Hills community.

FY 2024/25 CAGF-funded proposals can be organized under the following themes:

  •  Homeless Services – All Saints’ Episcopal Church (Home Again program/support services),
  Healthcare in Action (street medicine), and Safe Parking Los Angeles;
  •  Food Insecurity and Nutrition - Westside Food Bank, Our Big Kitchen Los Angeles, and
  Beverly Hills Community Farm;
  •  Senior Services – Affordable Living for the Aging (aging-in-place), Beverly Hills Active Adult
  Club (socialization), and OPICA (memory loss support);
  •  Health & Wellbeing – Our House (grief support), The Maple Counseling Center (mental
  health), Tower Cancer Research (cancer support), Saban Community Clinic (medical, dental),
  Cancer Support Community Los Angeles (cancer support), Chai Lifeline (emotional & financial
  support to families with ill children), ETTA (advocacy for young adults who are neurodiverse),
  NAMI (mental health), and The Miracle Project (social skills through theater programming for
  neurodiverse);
  •  Education – Beverly Hills Education Foundation (Student Intervention & Support Program);
  •  Cultural Enhancement – Theatre 40, Wallis Annenberg Center for the Performing Arts, Beverly
  Hills Theatre Guild, and the Farhang Foundation.

Council Liaisons recommended funding the twenty-three CAGF proposals for $1,113,500. Though no
longer entirely for CAGF recipients, it is important to note that the City’s General Fund is still
responsible for funding a total of $2,406,143 in social services, cultural grants, and critical service
provider agreements for the community.

Changes in the Community – Current and Future Needs
Needs of the Unhoused
Many conditions in Beverly Hills and society in general has changed since the CAGF program was first
created, which may render some legacy grants less impactful today than they were 20 years ago.
Additionally, many of the non-profit service providers can offer their services to Beverly Hills residents,
and regional residents, in need without receiving the corresponding funding from the City of Beverly
Hills.
One significant change observed by Human Services Division staff since the start of the pandemic in
2020 is the local and regional explosion in quantity and needs of people experiencing homelessness. In
late 2022 the City Council tasked staff with producing solutions and programs to manage the
homelessness crisis more aggressively and effectively.
Over the course of 2023, staff invested in a variety of ongoing services and programs to address
homelessness. Outreach services provided by Step Up were expanded to a total cost of $392,643,
software and mobile devices to track encounters with unhoused people totals $83,150, and Nastec
International, Inc. services were retained to manage the Outreach Hotline overnight and on weekends
and transport unhoused individuals to shelter or housing for $930,000. The five beds contracted with
PATH at the cost of $100,000 a year moved to a critical service provider agreement. Additionally,
returning CAGF partners such as All Saints Episcopal Church ($45,000), Safe Parking LA ($10,000),
and new CAGF partner Healthcare in Action ($100,000) are all providing services for the unhoused.

  3
10/30/2024 Social Services Liaisons
 The most impactful expense added in 2023 is a 10-year agreement for scattered-site permanent
supportive housing for up to 30 individuals, plus 120 nights of motel stays, and wrap around case
management services in the amount of $1,417,000 per year. When you add up these services for the
unhoused in Beverly Hills, it totals $3,078,495.
Prior to 2022, the City’s direct spending on homelessness services was $320,000, an additional
$2,758,495 has been invested per year since 2022. That additional investment in homelessness
services is $680,995 more than the entire 2023-24 CAGF awards of $2,077,500.

Unhoused Transport
Staff continues to evaluate the effectiveness of our programs and the return on investment for the
community, to ensure that services are being delivered in the most cost-effective manner possible. As
mentioned, the City contracts with Nastec International, Inc. for unhoused assistance services, which
includes answering the Outreach Hotline overnight and on weekends, responding to those calls or
dispatching the appropriate outreach team, and transporting unhoused individuals to a local motel.
Since November of 2022 when the Outreach Hotline launched, Nastec has fielded 539 calls out of a
total of 1,361 calls received, which averages out to 1.3 calls per day since the hotline launched. The
transporting of unhoused individuals overnight to a motel is a process that began in April of 2024, and
to-date, Nastec has transported 4 people. The cost to the City for these services is approximately
$930,000 per year.
As of the publishing of this report, the City has terminated the agreement with Nastec International, Inc.
and in working with Beverly Hills Police Department, staff has identified the ability of the existing
company that provides supplemental patrol services to add the management of the Outreach Hotline
and Unhoused Transport services at no additional cost. By transitioning service providers, the City no
longer needs to identify an additional $930,000 of funding, while maintaining the same level of service
to the community and unhoused individuals. Eliminating the need for $930,000 in additional funding for
the unhoused would result in total annual spending on unhoused services of $2,148,495.

Future Needs
The continued investment of over $2 million per year in services for the unhoused will be a necessary
expense to provide the humane and responsive resources needed to keep pace with the regional
homelessness crisis.
Additionally, staff has observed an increase in behavioral issues both among the unhoused population
but also in the youth population serviced by City staff operating afterschool programs and summer
camps. The ability and funding to contract for behavioral aids for afterschool programs would greatly
benefit all participants in this program. However, the City can no longer afford to provide over $2 million
in community grant funding in light of the over $2 million in direct services to the unhoused currently
being provided.
Staff recommends placing the Community Assistance Grant Funding program on hiatus for the 2025-26
program year, in which applications would be distributed in January 2025 for funding to start July 1,
2025.
The hiatus would allow staff time to evaluate the changes this year that moved five former-CAGF
partners from grant funding to an operational contract and determine if current levels of service were
adequately maintained. The hiatus would also allow staff to work with a few other current CAGF
partners to explore adding them to the list of critical service providers, to provide services as-needed,
from organizations like All Saints Episcopal Church, Healthcare in Action, or The Maple Counseling
Center, and get a better understanding of the community’s use of those services based on invoicing.
  4
10/30/2024 Social Services Liaisons
 Recommended Changes
It is very subjective and open to debate when evaluating the value of one grant-funded partner in
comparison to another. This is especially true when the process has been created over the years to
eliminate duplicative service providers, ensure resources are being utilized by Beverly Hills residents,
and provide a service that the City is not currently providing through staff or other contracted agencies.

That said, there are some variables that can help guide an evaluation process if the goal is to reduce
the overall CAGF budget, while taking steps to mitigate any unintended consequences. One variable is
the size and scope of the organization, are they able to continue to serve Beverly Hills residents, as
well as the region, without the grant from the City of Beverly Hills. Another variable is the amount of
Beverly Hills residents that make up their clientele, as many service providers serve the region, and so
the City’s grant-funding is supporting residents of other communities. An additional variable to consider
is how critical is the service being provided, and can residents acquire the services through their own
private medical insurance or Medicare/Medi-Cal, without additional investment from the City of Beverly
Hills.

We must also consider the potential impact to the community if a particular service is no longer being
provided by the City’s grant-funding. For example, of the clientele served by Tower Cancer Research’s
grant-funding, only 10% are Beverly Hills residents. Or OUR HOUSE Grief Support Center in which 41
of their 2,142 clients served in the previous fiscal year were Beverly Hills residents. Both organizations
are fantastic and provide a great service, but at this time, perhaps they can continue to serve those
Beverly Hills residents using their existing operating funds. As we place the CAGF program on hiatus, it
will allow staff to discover if Beverly Hills residents are no longer able to receive the services they
depend upon, and if that is the case, we can pursue bringing the organization back under a service-
based agreement with a not-to-exceed amount.

Grant Funding Hiatus
Utilizing the approach described above, staff recommends placing the grant funding for fiscal year
2025-26 on hiatus. The following organizations would no longer receive grant funding: Affordable Living
for the Aging, Beverly Hills Community Farm, Cancer Support Community LA, Chai Lifeline West
Coast, ETTA, NAMI, OPICA Adult Day Program, OUR HOUSE Grief Support Center, Saban
Community Clinic, Safe Parking LA, The Miracle Project, and Tower Cancer Research. A hiatus of
funding to these organizations would reduce the CAGF budget by $378,500.

Community Service Providers
At the same time that staff is recommending a hiatus for grant funding to some, there is a
recommendation that several other providers be transitioned to a contracted-community service
provider, and they can invoice the City for as-needed services, up to a not-to-exceed amount. Although
these organizations are not critical service providers, staff understands the importance to the
community of these cultural and community-based organizations.

Staff recommends entering into as-needed agreements with the following service providers: All Saints’
Homeless Assistance Program, Beverly Hills Theater Guild, Beverly Hills Active Adult Club, Farhang
Foundation, Our Big Kitchen LA, Healthcare in Action, OPICA Adult Day Program, The Maple
Counseling Center, Theater 40, Wallis Annenberg Center for the Performing Arts, and Westside Food
Bank.

  5
10/30/2024 Social Services Liaisons
 The Beverly Hills Education Foundation also receives grant funding, and it is recommended that their
funding be incorporated into the next Joint Powers Agreement between the City and the Beverly Hills
Unified School District.

All of these organizations are being recommended for a not-to-exceed contract for the same value as
their current FY24-25 CAGF award. One exception is Westside Food Bank in which the
recommendation is to reduce from a $250,000 grant to a $50,000 contract, to provide fresh produce
and food once a week to the residents in the City’s housing program.

The amount to contract with this group of organizations is $535,000. After reducing Westside Food
Bank from $250,000 to $50,000, the CAGF budget reduction from grants placed on hiatus increases
from $378,500 to $578,500.

FISCAL IMPACT
The total amount awarded to the twenty-three CAGF proposals in FY24-25 is $1,113,500. Placing
twelve of the twenty-three grants on hiatus in FY25-26 would result in savings of $578,500.
The total amount to contract with the five critical service providers for Fiscal Year 24/25 is $1,292,643.
Converting eleven of the current CAGF partners to as-needed, not-to-exceed community service
providers contracts for services would cost $535,000. That would increase the contracted total to
$1,827,643.
This realignment of service providers would result in at least $578,500 in savings, and potentially more
as the City will be invoiced for services rendered rather than issuing the full grant amount.

RECOMMENDATION
Staff recommends placing the Community Assistance Grant Funding for Fiscal Year 2025-26 on hiatus;
converting eleven of the current CAGF partners to as-needed, not-to-exceed community service
provider contracts for services; and increasing the amount of service providers contracted to sixteen at
a total cost of $1,827,643.
